title: Vatican II lived
hookLine: Mass in local languages, the priest facing the people, more of the Bible read aloud

cards: Ask an older Catholic what Sunday Mass sounded like when they were small, and some will describe the same scene.
The priest stood at an altar against the far wall, his back to the people, praying in Latin, much of it quietly.
In the pews, some followed in a missal with the translation printed beside it; others prayed the rosary on their own. Then, within a few years, the same parish changed. The priest turned around.
He said The Lord be with you in English, or Spanish, or Tagalog. Lay people walked up to read. Bishops in Rome had met and written documents.

teach.b: The Second Vatican Council's document on the liturgy is known by its opening Latin words, Sacrosanctum Concilium. Here's what it changed, and what it didn't. First, the language.
It allowed the Mass and the sacraments to be celebrated more widely in the people's own languages.
Catholics sometimes hear Pentecost in that, when the crowd in Jerusalem was amazed because, in the Douay-Rheims, "every man heard them speak in his own tongue." Second, the Bible.

teach.h: MORE OF THE BIBLE, READ ALOUD.
teach.b: It asks that the treasures of Scripture be opened up more richly, so more of the Bible is read aloud at Mass. Third, the people.
It speaks of the faithful taking part fully and actively, not as silent spectators. So lay people began to read, to sing the responses, to bring up the gifts. Fourth, the surprises.
The document doesn't actually tell priests to turn the altar around; that came in the reforms that followed. It doesn't abolish Latin either.
It says Latin is to be kept, and gives Gregorian chant a place of honor. Catholics still differ about all this.

teach.h: EVERY MAN HEARD THEM SPEAK IN HIS OWN TONGUE.
teach.b: Some love the reformed Mass in their own language. Some are drawn to the older Latin form and attend it where it's allowed. And for some, Vatican II isn't first a document at all.
It's the Sunday the priest turned around.

how: Catholic parishes generally celebrate Mass in the local language with the priest facing the people and lay readers proclaiming the first readings; in some places the older Latin form is also celebrated with the bishop's permission.

o: the Vatican II document that reshaped the Mass
the Latin prayer that opens a sung Mass
a council decree that banned Latin at Mass

games.q: Vatican II lived — tap the pairs.
p: the council's document on the liturgy

s: Vatican II abolished Latin in the Mass
its liturgy document says Latin is to be kept, while allowing local languages.
the council's document orders the altar turned toward the people
that came in the reforms that followed, not in the document itself.
the document asks for more of the Bible to be read aloud
it asks that the treasures of Scripture be opened up more richly.

games.q: you're a bishop at the council. people in the pews can't follow the Latin. what do you write?
o: keep Latin, and allow the people's own languages more widely.
change nothing; the people have their missals.
games.why: the document did both: Latin is to be kept, and local languages may be used more widely.

practice: Walk through a Mass you've been to, in your mind, or any church you've stood in: where the altar is, which way the priest faces, what language you hear, who walks up to read.
Find one thing the council touched and one thing that stayed old, a hymn, a statue, a Latin word that survived. If you pray, pray for that parish as it is now; if not, simply hold the room in mind.

wordCard.voice: Sacrosanctum Concilium. The Second Vatican Council's document on the liturgy, which opened the Mass to people's own languages and asked the faithful to take part fully and actively.

orig.note: Latin: this sacred council, the opening words of Vatican II's document on the liturgy.

carryVoice: Your line: the council in the pews. A document from Rome, felt first on a Sunday morning. Day nine hundred eighteen, done.
